messages.content:
Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Generator scaffolding left in: oaicite, [cite: 1], placeholders -- finish the text and read it
- The "it's not X, it's Y" construction -- just state Y
- A bolded word opening a list item as a per-item tag -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- Saying "is" the long way: serves as, boasts, functions as -- use the plain verb
- One-line dramatic fragments: "That's it. That's the whole thing." -- cut them, the preceding sentence already made the point
- Em dashes clustering in one document -- most drafts need 0-2; use commas, periods or parentheses for the rest
- Filler verbs: leverages, facilitates, unlocks -- use a plain verb, or cut the sentence
- A snake_case identifier written as plain prose -- name it in words, or mark it as inline code
- Marketing cliches: "hidden gem", "let's dive in" -- say the specific thing
- The "Not X. Not Y." listing construction -- state the point once
- Stock section skeleton: "Despite its success", "Looking ahead" -- name the specific thing the section is for
- Standalone filler adverbs: undoubtedly, arguably, notably, importantly, ultimately -- most add nothing; cut them unless one is carrying real emphasis
- A banned synonym of one of this project's canonical terms, per its declared lexicon -- one word, one meaning: use the canonical term the word's own note names
- Dramatic turning points with nothing concrete behind them: "Everything changed." -- name the actual event, or cut it

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write a post about what a software company learned from a year of remote work. Around 250 words.

A year ago we shut the office and told everyone to work from wherever they had a chair and a wifi signal. We expected a dip in output and a slow crawl back to normal. Neither happened the way we predicted.

Meetings were doing less work than we thought. Cutting the standing weekly sync and replacing it with a written update in Slack saved four hours a week per engineer, and nobody missed the meeting. We now default to async updates and reserve video calls for decisions that need real back-and-forth.

Our onboarding process depended on hallway osmosis we never wrote down. New hires who joined remotely in the first few months struggled to find basic answers, because those answers lived in people's heads, not in docs. We spent the spring rewriting our internal wiki, and time-to-first-commit for new engineers dropped from three weeks to eight days.

Harder to admit: some of our best collaboration happened in person, by accident, and no tool replaces it. We now fly the whole engineering team in twice a year for a week of planning and pairing. Attendance is optional but almost everyone comes.

Revenue held steady. Turnover dropped. The office lease is gone, and most of the team says they would not go back to five days a week even if we asked.

We are not claiming remote work fixed everything. It forced us to write down what used to live in the walls, and the writing turned out to be worth keeping.

The text above has these problems. Rewrite it so none remain.
Change nothing else, and keep the same length and purpose.

- colon_reveal (Harder to admit:):
- paragraph_uniformity (6 paragraphs, spread 0.25):

Return only the rewritten text.

output:
A year ago we shut the office and told everyone to work from wherever they had a chair and a wifi signal. We expected a dip in output and a slow crawl back to normal. Neither happened the way we predicted.

Meetings were doing less work than we thought. Cutting the standing weekly sync and replacing it with a written update in Slack saved four hours a week per engineer, and nobody missed the meeting. We now default to async updates and reserve video calls for decisions that need real back-and-forth.

Our onboarding process depended on hallway osmosis we never wrote down. New hires who joined remotely in the first few months struggled to find basic answers, because those answers lived in people's heads, not in docs. We spent the spring rewriting our internal wiki, and time-to-first-commit for new engineers dropped from three weeks to eight days.

Some of our best collaboration happened in person, by accident, and no tool replaces it. That was the hardest thing to admit, since it argued against everything else we were doing. We now fly the whole engineering team in twice a year for a week of planning and pairing. Attendance is optional but almost everyone comes, and the two trips have become the weeks people plan their vacations around.

Revenue held steady through the transition, and turnover dropped as people stopped commuting and started keeping their evenings. The office lease is gone. Most of the team says they would not go back to five days a week even if we asked, and a few have said they would leave if we did.

We are not claiming remote work fixed everything, but it forced us to write down what used to live in the walls, and the writing turned out to be worth keeping.
